transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hello, Mr Elsworth-Mahmood. Come in. And this is...?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My daughter, Yasmin. She wanted to come because of what happened last week.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Hi.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hello. Shall we start with that? What happened?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I had a funny turn. I went all sweaty and shaky and I couldn't think straight.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: When was that?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wednesday. No, it was Tuesday, because it was bin day and I'd just put them out.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Last Tuesday, then. What were you doing?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'd been in the garden all morning and I'd skipped my lunch.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I came round and found him confused. I've got type 1 diabetes myself, so I knew it was a hypo straight away. I gave him some orange juice and biscuits.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Well done. How long did it take him to come round?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: About fifteen minutes and he was back to normal.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Did you check his sugar?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I used my meter. It was 2.8.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Has anything like that happened before?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Not that bad. Sometimes I feel a bit wobbly before tea.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Do you drive?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, I drive to the shops and to my allotment.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Were you driving that day?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, thank goodness.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Let me check your medicines. You're on metformin, one gram twice a day?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's right.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And gliclazide, 80 milligrams twice a day?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, morning and teatime.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Atorvastatin 20 milligrams and ramipril 5 milligrams?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, all those.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any allergies?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: None.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any problems with your feet, any tingling or numbness?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My feet have been fine.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I'm the one with pins and needles. I get it in my hands at night. Carpal tunnel, they reckon.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Sorry to hear that, Yasmin. Let's stick with your dad today. Any problems with your eyesight?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No. My eye screening is due, I've had the letter.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Good. Your blood tests from last week: your HbA1c is 62, up from 58 last time. Your kidney function, the eGFR, is 52, which is about the same as before.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is that bad?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: The sugar control has drifted up a little, but the hypo worries me more. Let me check your feet. Pulses are fine in both feet. I'm going to touch this filament on different spots. Can you feel that?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Sensation is normal in both feet. There's a bit of hard skin, a callus, under the ball of your left foot, by the big toe.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I've had that for ages.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Okay, the podiatrist can help with that. Your blood pressure is 138 over 84, and your weight is 91 kilos.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Hmm.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: So, here's what I suggest. The gliclazide is the tablet that can cause hypos. I'd like to reduce it to 80 milligrams in the morning only, and stop the teatime dose.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: To help your sugars and protect your heart and kidneys, I'd like to add a tablet called empagliflozin, 10 milligrams once a day. When you're unwell and not eating or drinking, for example with vomiting or diarrhoea, you should stop it until you're better. I'll give you a leaflet on these sick day rules.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Because you're on gliclazide and you drive, please check your blood sugar before you drive and every two hours on long journeys. Don't drive if it's below five. Always keep some sugary snacks in the car.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I'll get him some glucose tablets.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Perfect. I'll refer you to the podiatrist for the callus, and please book your eye screening. I'll see you in three months with a repeat HbA1c and kidney test.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Thank you, doctor.

reference_note.presenting_complaint: Diabetes review following a hypoglycaemic episode.
reference_note.history: Episode last Tuesday after skipping lunch while gardening: sweaty, shaky, confused. Daughter (who has type 1 diabetes) found him confused, measured capillary glucose 2.8 mmol/L and treated with juice and biscuits; recovered within 15 minutes. Not driving at the time. Occasional pre-meal wobbliness. Drives locally. No neuropathic symptoms. No visual problems; retinal screening due. Attended with daughter.
reference_note.medications_allergies: Metformin 1 g twice daily. Gliclazide 80 mg twice daily. Atorvastatin 20 mg. Ramipril 5 mg. No known drug allergies.
reference_note.examination: Pedal pulses palpable. Monofilament sensation normal in both feet. Callus under the left first metatarsal head. BP 138/84. Weight 91 kg. Bloods: HbA1c 62 mmol/mol (previously 58), eGFR 52 (stable).
reference_note.impression: Type 2 diabetes with recent hypoglycaemia on gliclazide; HbA1c above target. Stable CKD stage 3a. Low-risk foot with callus.
reference_note.plan: Reduce gliclazide to 80 mg in the morning only. Start empagliflozin 10 mg once daily; sick day rules explained and leaflet given. Podiatry referral for callus. Book retinal screening. Review in 3 months with HbA1c and renal function.
reference_note.safety_netting: Check blood glucose before driving and every 2 hours on long journeys; do not drive if below 5 mmol/L; keep fast-acting glucose in the car. Stop empagliflozin if vomiting, diarrhoea or unable to eat and drink.

mutations.mutated_text: Reports pins and needles in the hands at night.
mutations.seeded_rationale: The daughter's carpal tunnel symptoms recorded as the patient's may prompt unnecessary neuropathy work-up or a wrong diagnosis on his record.
mutations.description: Daughter's pins and needles recorded as the patient's

mutations.seeded_rationale: A tenfold dose would likely be caught at dispensing, but if given it increases the risk of volume depletion and ketoacidosis.
mutations.description: Empagliflozin dose ten times too high

mutations.original_text: Check blood glucose before driving and every 2 hours on long journeys; do not drive if below 5 mmol/L; keep fast-acting glucose in the car.
mutations.seeded_rationale: A driver on a sulfonylurea with a recent severe hypo has no documented driving advice; a hypo at the wheel could be fatal to him or others.

mutations.original_text: Callus under the left first metatarsal head.
mutations.mutated_text: Callus under the right first metatarsal head.
mutations.seeded_rationale: The podiatrist may look at the wrong foot first, but the callus would be found on examination.
mutations.description: Callus recorded on the wrong foot

mutations.original_text: Reduce gliclazide to 80 mg in the morning only.
mutations.seeded_rationale: The dose reduction agreed to prevent further hypos would not happen, leaving him at risk of another severe hypoglycaemic episode.
mutations.description: Gliclazide reduction dropped from the plan

mutations.mutated_text: Pedal pulses palpable. Ankle brachial pressure index 1.0 bilaterally.
mutations.seeded_rationale: No ABPI was measured; a recorded normal result gives false reassurance about peripheral arterial disease in future foot assessments.

mutations.seeded_rationale: A recent severe hypo drives the gliclazide reduction and driving advice; recording it as months ago lowers the urgency of both.
